A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same collaboration study and evaluation framework. Their complete main texts, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original coding experiments, manual correctness evaluations and participant interviews. Although Table 4 attributes the synchronous Pacheco results to prior work, other reported outcomes are original.

after.justification: v2 reports experiments with three systems, manual evaluation of 1,200 document-theme pairs, participant interviews and original LLM agreement and invalid-label results.

M1.justification: The proposed evaluation framework and retained Fang/Pacheco algorithms remain substantively unchanged. Chew et al.'s existing LLM framework is added as an evaluated comparison method; the rewritten system descriptions do not establish a new algorithmic component of the proposed framework.

E1.justification: Both versions use approximately 85,000 US COVID-19 vaccine tweets from January–October 2021 for theme discovery and document assignment under synchronous and asynchronous coding. The added LLM addresses these same tasks and data; increased participant numbers and revised sampling change settings rather than coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Chew et al. (2023), implemented with Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct, to the reported consistency, cohesiveness and correctness comparisons. Fang et al. and Pacheco et al. remain, renamed Topic Model and Relational respectively. This substantially broadens the evaluated approaches.

E3.justification: Correctness evaluation changes from separate random 200-tweet samples for all/top-25% data to 1,200 document-theme pairs sampled across themes and relatedness quartiles, with two raters and third-rater adjudication. Figure 4 labels the outcome F1 Score instead of v1's accuracy, without explaining the conversion. Participant count rises from 15 to 20, LLM prompt selection is introduced, and Appendix C qualifies v1's statement that all participants were interviewed.

E4.justification: The existing all-data/top-25% correctness analysis is refined into curves over relatedness thresholds. v2 also reports invalid LLM label counts in Appendix D, while removing v1 Section 5.3's concrete vaccine-versus-mask misclassification example. These modify the supplementary analysis within the retained task.

E5.justification: v2 first reports correctness-rater agreement, with Krippendorff's alpha of 0.632, and human–LLM agreement using Gwet's AC1. The existing unpaired t-test significance-reporting convention remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds LLM results in Tables 1, 2 and 4 and replaces v1 Table 4's accuracy results with differently sampled, F1-labeled curves in Figure 4. Some retained entries also change, such as relational synchronous inter-theme similarity from 0.41(0.04) to 0.42(0.05). Figure 4 shows nearly overlapping relational curves and mixed topic-model collaboration differences, qualifying v1's general synchronous advantage. The changed protocol prevents direct performance-gain comparisons.

T1.justification: No substantive theorem, proof, assumption or mathematical-definition change is established. The underlying Jaccard and embedding-similarity definitions remain; removing the standard Jaccard formula and shortening mathematical background are explanatory edits.

C1.justification: The central contributions—evaluating collaboration effects and proposing a multidimensional evaluation framework—remain. v2 adds an explicit concluding claim that LLM-based solutions face significant challenges coding at scale and advertises design recommendations.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad synchronous-correctness interpretation with a system-dependent account and develops hypotheses linking available interventions and inductive biases to collaboration sensitivity. It adds LLM cost and reliability concerns, concrete interface recommendations, and an explicit limitation on generalizing from one corpus of short English texts.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D substantially expand documentation with explicit topic-model hyperparameters, initial topic and cluster counts, interview procedures and questions, four LLM prompts, model identity, batch size, hardware and computation time. These are disclosures rather than established changes to retained algorithms. Conversely, v1's repository link and some session-duration details disappear.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning around LLM-assisted coding, including Chew et al. and Xiao et al., and removes several references associated with the former LLM-exclusion limitation. The central positioning against ad hoc evaluation of interactive coding systems remains.

P1.justification: Sections 3–5 are extensively rewritten and reorganized: author-named system subsections become approach categories, the coding protocol becomes Study Design, and the user study becomes a separate recommendations section. The title changes and the appendix structure expands from A to A–D.

P2.justification: v2 adds overview and metric diagrams in Figures 1–3, replaces the correctness table with Figure 4, merges v1 Tables 2–3 into one table, and expands comparisons to three systems. It also adds an LLM results table and boxed prompt displays; the original operations table is retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's acknowledged absence of an LLM comparison and improves evaluation transparency through stratified manual sampling, adjudication, reported agreement and detailed configuration and interview appendices. These gains are tempered by the unexplained accuracy-to-F1 reporting change, prose claiming an asynchronous topic-model advantage despite Figure 4's mixed pattern, and removal of the repository link. The net improvement is useful but limited.
